{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. The repo shows the identical pattern in shell, TypeScript+Bun, and Python+UV. The agent stops being a chat window and becomes a component you embed anywhere in the software development lifecycle.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is also a programmable Agentic Coding tool... we can run it from any programming language that has terminal access... we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle.\"",
      "misconception": "That the demo scripts are trivial wrappers not worth running ('I already watched Dan do it'). The scripts ARE the lesson: it's not just about the agentic prompt, it's about where you can use it — including full agentic environments where you're not even present."
    },
    {
      "id": "systems-that-build-systems",
      "name": "Systems that build systems / self-operating codebase",
      "plain_english": "The end-state: codebases that increasingly run themselves — agents firing at the right time, doing the right work, with and without your oversight. Lesson 1 plants the seed (a scripted agent that does a full branch-write-run-commit-report cycle); the rest of TAC scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"The irreplaceable engineer in phase two that we're aiming to become is the engineer that transforms their code bases into self-operating machines... so much so that your code base literally runs itself.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is hype about full autonomy tomorrow. The lesson's actual claim is incremental: 'increasingly self-operating,' built by investing your time in the right places and repeatedly extracting value."
    },
    {
      "id": "engineer-not-coder",
      "name": "You're an engineer, not a coder",
      "plain_english": "Engineering was never about writing code; it's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for users and customers. Code is one asset those systems produce. This reframe is what makes 'stop coding' coherent rather than self-destructive.",
      "dan_words": "\"Engineering was never about writing code. It's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for your users and your customers... Remember, you're an engineer, not a coder. The difference is massive.\"",
      "misconception": "That leverage means working more hours with AI. The 10x engineer emerges from 10x leverage, not 10x time or effort — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 10x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find."
    },
    {
      "id": "replace-yourself",
      "name": "To become irreplaceable, replace yourself",
      "plain_english": "The lesson's closing paradox: the engineer who systematically automates their own work (replaces themselves) becomes the one the org can't replace — because they're the one who builds and commands the automation. Vibe coders can't replicate this.",
      "dan_words": "\"The contradicting truth about what you'll learn in tactical agentic coding is this: To become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.\"",
      "misconception": "Reading it as job-loss fatalism. It's the opposite — an asymmetric-advantage strategy: in the tech industry, all the alpha lies in the future, in pushing what's possible forward."
    }
  ],

# Success is Planned: The 80-20 of Agentic Coding
**Lesson #3 (Intermediate)**  ·  https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/success-is-planned

_First came prompts, then came plans and what comes next will push your ability to hand off work to your agents even further beyond. Learn a powerful leverage point of agentic coding that enables your agents to ship with you and your team's engineering best practices._

## Loot Box — 22 notes

### 🔥 The Prompt is Everything
What was once a complete joke is now the most valuable skill any engineer can have. The prompt is the medium through which you communicate to your agentic tools and all generative AI technology.

### 🔥 Plans Are Scaled Prompts
A scaled prompt is a plan, a specification, a PRD. Plans are prompts scaled up for high impact. Great planning is great prompting - they are one and the same.

### 🔥 Success is Planned
Those who plan the future tend to create it. Success is planned. In this lesson, we enter the plan and build phase of the agentic software developer lifecycle.

### 🔥 The 80-20 of Agentic Coding
With just three tactics (Stop Coding, Adopt Agent's Perspective, Template Your Engineering), you'll learn the Pareto 80-20 of agentic engineering. These fundamentals deliver 80% of the impact with 20% of the complexity.

### 🏆 Tactic #3: Template Your Engineering
When you template your engineering, you encode your engineering workflows and best practices into reusable, scalable units of agentic success. By encoding your problem-solving patterns into templates, you create a living library of engineering expertise that your agents can consistently execute with high precision across sets of problems.

### 🔥 Solving Problem Classes, Not Problems
Templates enable you to solve entire classes of problems, not just individual problems. Create templates for chores, bugs, features, and refactors that work consistently across any codebase.

### 🔥 Templates for Team Leverage
Templates create leverage not just for you, but for your entire team. Your engineering expertise becomes a shared resource that everyone can access, use, and improve.

### 🔥 Planning Alone is Expensive
Planning is time consuming and there's always something to miss. The time planning consumes scales with the difficulty of the problem and the size and complexity of your codebase. Templates solve this problem.

### 🔥 Templates Encode Problem Solving
Templates let us encode problem solving into reusable units that work on small to large codebases. They can handle chores, bugs, small features, large features, new codebases, all the way up to massive refactors.

### ⚔️ TAC Lesson 3 - Success is Planned Repository
git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-3.git

### 🔥 Reusable Prompts as Time Savers
Reusable prompts and templates are extremely powerful time savers due to how reusable they are - not just for you, but for your entire team. They encode engineering expertise once, execute infinitely.

### ⚙️ Chore Template Command
/chore "your chore description"

### 🔥 Meta-Prompts: Prompts That Build Prompts
A meta-prompt is a prompt that builds a prompt. This agentic prompt builds a plan based on a template that your agent fills out. This is extremely powerful - not only should we stop coding, we should also leverage our agents to write plans with us and for us.

### 🔥 Plans Written to Specs Directory
All generated plans are written to the specs directory. These plans contain chore descriptions, relevant files, step-by-step tasks, validation commands, and implementation notes.

### 🔥 Built-in Validation Commands
Every plan includes validation commands that verify the work was completed successfully. This creates a closed-loop system where agents can self-validate their implementations.

### 🔥 From One Line to Comprehensive Plan
With templates, you write one high-level sentence and get an entire comprehensive plan. This scales your impact exponentially - turning simple ideas into detailed, executable specifications.

### 🔥 Anatomy of a Template
Every great template contains: Purpose at the top, detailed instructions, relevant files to guide success, plan format in markdown, and a parameter that accepts your high-level description.

### 🔥 Now We Can Template Our Engineering
By using meta-prompts and templates, we can now template our engineering. This fundamentally changes your engineering impact by encoding problem-solving patterns into reusable units.

### ⚙️ Implement Plan Command
/implement specs/your-plan.md

### 🔥 Activating Reasoning with "Think Hard"
The "think hard" instruction activates Claude Code's reasoning model. This is one of the 12 leverage points of agentic coding - turning on the reasoning model for complex problem solving.

### 🔥 Higher-Order Prompts (HOPs)
A Higher-Order Prompt accepts another prompt as input. When you pass a plan into the implement command, you're using a HOP - plans getting passed into plans. This enables powerful prompt composition.

### 🔥 Aligning Plans with Agent Capabilities
We're leveraging our plan and aligning it with the capabilities of our agent. The to-do list created by the agent lines up perfectly with the step-by-step breakdown in our plan. Create a new plan in specs/*.md to resolve the `Bug` using the exact specified markdown `Plan Format`. Follow the `Instructions` to create the plan use the `Relevant Files` to focus on the right files.

## Instructions

- You're writing a plan to resolve a bug, it should be thorough and precise so we fix the root cause and prevent regressions.
- Create the plan in the `specs/*.md` file. Name it appropriately based on the `Bug`.
- Use the plan format below to create the plan. 
- Research the codebase to understand the bug, reproduce it, and put together a plan to fix it.
- IMPORTANT: Replace every <placeholder> in the `Plan Format` with the requested value. Add as much detail as needed to fix the bug.
- Use your reasoning model: THINK HARD about the bug, its root cause, and the steps to fix it properly.
- IMPORTANT: Be surgical with your bug fix, solve the bug at hand and don't fall off track.
- IMPORTANT: We want the minimal number of changes that will fix and address the bug.
- Don't use decorators. Keep it simple.
- If you need a new library, use `uv add` and be sure to report it in the `Notes` section of the `Plan Format`.
- Respect requested files in the `Relevant Files` section.
- Start your research by reading the `README.md` file.

## Relevant Files

Focus on the following files:
- `README.md` - Contains the project overview and instructions.
- `app/**` - Contains the codebase client/server.
- `scripts/**` - Contains the scripts to start and stop the server + client.

Ignore all other files in the codebase.

## Plan Format

```md
# Bug: <bug name>

## Bug Description
<describe the bug in detail, including symptoms and expected vs actual behavior>

## Problem Statement
<clearly define the specific problem that needs to be solved>

## Solution Statement
<describe the proposed solution approach to fix the bug>

## Steps to Reproduce
<list exact steps to reproduce the bug>

## Root Cause Analysis
<analyze and explain the root cause of the bug>

## Relevant Files
Use these files to fix the bug:

<find and list the files that are relevant to the bug describe why they are relevant in bullet points. If there are new files that need to be created to fix the bug, list them in an h3 'New Files' section.>

## Step by Step Tasks
IMPORTANT: Execute every step in order, top to bottom.

<list step by step tasks as h3 headers plus bullet points. use as many h3 headers as needed to fix the bug. Order matters, start with the foundational shared changes required to fix the bug then move on to the specific changes required to fix the bug. Include tests that will validate the bug is fixed with zero regressions. Your last step should be running the `Validation Commands` to validate the bug is fixed with zero regressions.>

## Validation Commands
Execute every command to validate the bug is fixed with zero regressions.

<list commands you'll use to validate with 100% confidence the bug is fixed with zero regressions. every command must execute without errors so be specific about what you want to run to validate the bug is fixed with zero regressions. Include commands to reproduce the bug before and after the fix.>
- `cd app/server && uv run pytest` - Run server tests to validate the bug is fixed with zero regressions

## Notes
<optionally list any additional notes or context that are relevant to the bug that will be helpful to the developer>
```

## Bug

# Natural Language SQL Interface

A web application that converts natural language queries to SQL using AI, built with FastAPI and Vite + TypeScript.

## Features

- 🗣️ Natural language to SQL conversion using OpenAI or Anthropic
- 📁 Drag-and-drop file upload (.csv and .json)
- 📊 Interactive table results display
- 🔒 SQL injection protection
- ⚡ Fast development with Vite and uv

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.10+
- Node.js 18+
- OpenAI API key and/or Anthropic API key

## Setup

### 1. Install Dependencies

```bash
# Backend
cd app/server
uv sync --all-extras

# Frontend
cd app/client
npm install
```

### 2. Environment Configuration

Set up your API keys in the root and the server directory:

```bash
cp .env.sample .env
```

and

```bash
cd app/server
cp .env.sample .env
# Edit .env and add your API keys
```


## Quick Start

Use the provided script to start both services:

```bash
./scripts/start.sh
```

Press `Ctrl+C` to stop both services.

The script will:
- Check that `.env` exists in `app/server/`
- Start the backend on http://localhost:8000
- Start the frontend on http://localhost:5173
- Handle graceful shutdown when you exit

## Manual Start (Alternative)

### Backend
```bash
cd app/server
# .env is loaded automatically by python-dotenv
uv run python server.py
```

### Frontend
```bash
cd app/client
npm run dev
```

## Usage

1. **Upload Data**: Click "Upload Data" to open the modal
   - Use sample data buttons for quick testing
   - Or drag and drop your own .csv or .json files
   - Uploading a file with the same name will overwrite the existing table
2. **Query Your Data**: Type a natural language query like "Show me all users who signed up last week"
   - Press `Cmd+Enter` (Mac) or `Ctrl+Enter` (Windows/Linux) to run the query
3. **View Results**: See the generated SQL and results in a table format
4. **Manage Tables**: Click the × button on any table to remove it

## Development

### Backend Commands
```bash
cd app/server
uv run python server.py      # Start server with hot reload
uv run pytest               # Run tests
uv add <package>            # Add package to project
uv remove <package>         # Remove package from project
uv sync --all-extras        # Sync all extras
```

### Frontend Commands
```bash
cd app/client
npm run dev                 # Start dev server
npm run build              # Build for production
npm run preview            # Preview production build
```

## Project Structure

```
app/
├── client/                 # Vite + TypeScript frontend
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── api/           # API client
│   │   ├── types.d.ts     # TypeScript types
│   │   └── main.ts        # App entry point
│   └── vite.config.ts     # Vite configuration
│
└── server/                # FastAPI backend
    ├── core/              # Core modules
    │   ├── data_models.py # Pydantic models
    │   ├── file_processor.py
    │   ├── llm_processor.py
    │   ├── sql_processor.py
    │   └── insights.py
    ├── db/                # SQLite database
    └── server.py          # FastAPI app
```

## API Endpoints

- `POST /api/upload` - Upload CSV/JSON file
- `POST /api/query` - Process natural language query
- `GET /api/schema` - Get database schema
- `POST /api/insights` - Generate column insights
- `GET /api/health` - Health check

## Security

- Only SELECT queries are allowed
- SQL injection protection via keyword blocking
- File upload validation
- CORS configured for local development

## Troubleshooting

**Backend won't start:**
- Check Python version: `python --version` (requires 3.12+)
- Verify API keys are set: `echo $OPENAI_API_KEY`

**Frontend errors:**
- Clear node_modules: `rm -rf node_modules && npm install`
- Check Node version: `node --version` (requires 18+)

**CORS issues:**
- Ensure backend is running on port 8000
- Check vite.config.ts proxy settings

==> scripts/start.sh <==
#!/bin/bash

# Colors for output
GREEN='\033[0;32m'
BLUE='\033[0;34m'
RED='\033[0;31m'
NC='\033[0m' # No Color

echo -e "${BLUE}Starting Natural Language SQL Interface...${NC}"

# Get the script's directory
SCRIPT_DIR="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" && pwd )"
PROJECT_ROOT="$( dirname "$SCRIPT_DIR" )"

# Check if .env exists in server directory
if [ ! -f "$PROJECT_ROOT/app/server/.env" ]; then
    echo -e "${RED}Warning: No .env file found in app/server/.${NC}"
    echo "Please:"
    echo "  1. cd app/server"
    echo "  2. cp .env.sample .env"
    echo "  3. Edit .env and add your API keys"
    exit 1
fi

# Function to cleanup on exit
cleanup() {
    echo -e "\n${BLUE}Shutting down services...${NC}"
    
    # Kill all child processes
    jobs -p | xargs -r kill 2>/dev/null
    
    # Wait for processes to terminate
    wait
    
    echo -e "${GREEN}Services stopped successfully.${NC}"
    exit 0
}

# Trap EXIT, INT, and TERM signals
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

#!/bin/bash

# Colors for output
GREEN='\033[0;32m'
BLUE='\033[0;34m'
RED='\033[0;31m'
NC='\033[0m' # No Color

echo -e "${BLUE}Stopping Natural Language SQL Interface...${NC}"

# Kill any running start.sh processes
echo -e "${GREEN}Killing start.sh processes...${NC}"
pkill -f "start.sh" 2>/dev/null

# Kill processes on specific ports
echo -e "${GREEN}Killing processes on ports 5173 and 8000...${NC}"
lsof -ti:5173,8000 | xargs kill -9 2>/dev/null

echo -e "${GREEN}✓ Services stopped successfully!${NC}"

#!/bin/bash

# Colors for output
GREEN='\033[0;32m'
BLUE='\033[0;34m'
RED='\033[0;31m'
NC='\033[0m' # No Color

echo -e "${BLUE}Starting Natural Language SQL Interface...${NC}"

# Get the script's directory
SCRIPT_DIR="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" && pwd )"
PROJECT_ROOT="$( dirname "$SCRIPT_DIR" )"

# Check if .env exists in server directory
if [ ! -f "$PROJECT_ROOT/app/server/.env" ]; then
    echo -e "${RED}Warning: No .env file found in app/server/.${NC}"
    echo "Please:"
    echo "  1. cd app/server"
    echo "  2. cp .env.sample .env"
    echo "  3. Edit .env and add your API keys"
    exit 1
fi

# Function to cleanup on exit
cleanup() {
    echo -e "\n${BLUE}Shutting down services...${NC}"
    
    # Kill all child processes
    jobs -p | xargs -r kill 2>/dev/null
    
    # Wait for processes to terminate
    wait
    
    echo -e "${GREEN}Services stopped successfully.${NC}"
    exit 0
}

# Trap EXIT, INT, and TERM signals
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

            sql = sql[3:]
        if sql.endswith("```"):

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "What was once a complete joke is now the most valuable skill any engineer can have. The prompt is everything.", "approx_timestamp": "0:18" },
    { "text": "It's a plan. It's a specification. It's a PRD. Plans are prompts scaled up for high impact.", "approx_timestamp": "1:46" },
    { "text": "The plan is the prompt. And that means great planning is great prompting.", "approx_timestamp": "1:52" },
    { "text": "Those who plan the future tend to create it. Success is planned.", "approx_timestamp": "2:46" },
    { "text": "With just three tactics, you'll learn the Pareto 80/20 of agentic engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "2:59" },
    { "text": "When you template your engineering, you encode your problem solving into reusable units that you, your team, and your agents can see, use, and importantly, improve.", "approx_timestamp": "3:40" },
    { "text": "What is a meta prompt? It's a prompt that builds a prompt.", "approx_timestamp": "8:04" },
    { "text": "Not only should we stop coding, we should also lean into and leverage our agent to write plans with us and for us.", "approx_timestamp": "11:40" },
    { "text": "It doesn't take a lot to do a lot, but you need the right information.", "approx_timestamp": "12:40" },
    { "text": "This is a higher order prompt, AKA a hop.", "approx_timestamp": "13:34" },
    { "text": "Don't limit yourself. Don't make the mistake in thinking that Gen AI can't solve your problem in a major way.", "approx_timestamp": "18:19" },
    { "text": "Why do I keep opening up new Claude Code instances?... I keep opening new terminals and starting fresh agent instances that have no memory of what just happened.", "approx_timestamp": "23:03" },
    { "text": "We force our prompts, plans and templates to be isolated, reusable, and improvable assets with zero dependencies.", "approx_timestamp": "25:34" },
    { "text": "Remember, we're not here to babysit a single agent.", "approx_timestamp": "25:55" },
    { "text": "We need to decouple our performance from the conversational context window.", "approx_timestamp": "26:26" },
    { "text": "We want one shot successes.", "approx_timestamp": "26:32" },
    { "text": "This is the power of templating your engineering. I still haven't lifted a finger.", "approx_timestamp": "30:24" },
    { "text": "Having agents run loose on your code base without structure, without knowing how you do things is a plan for failure.", "approx_timestamp": "30:58" },
    { "text": "You want to be building the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "38:45" },
    { "text": "You can also think of your plans as staging environments for code that will be generated.", "approx_timestamp": "39:55" },
    { "text": "Be very careful thinking that these tactics can't work for you and on your codebase. That is a limiting belief.", "approx_timestamp": "44:20" },
    { "text": "I'll see you in lesson four where we'll learn to let your product ship itself.", "approx_timestamp": "46:29" }

  "what_student_must_internalize": [
    "The plan IS the prompt. A plan/spec/PRD is a prompt scaled up for high impact — so great planning is literally great prompting, not a separate discipline.",
    "Templates encode problem-solving for CLASSES of work, not instances. /chore, /bug, /feature each encode a different process; the output of a template is always a plan in specs/, never code.",
    "A meta prompt is a prompt that builds a prompt; a higher order prompt (HOP) is a prompt that takes prompts as input. Template → plan → /implement(plan) is meta-prompting composed with a HOP.",
    "Two prompts, two phases, two agents: planning and building are separate SDLC nodes run by separate fresh instances. The chore was completed 'agentically with two prompts, one for the planning phase and one for the coding building phase.'",
    "The three reasons for fresh agents: context focus; isolated/reusable/improvable zero-dependency assets; preparation for off-device runs. Decouple performance from the conversational context window; aim for one-shot successes.",
    "At boot you should know 100% of your agent's context (the HOP file + the plan file). That certainty is what makes failures diagnosable and templates improvable.",
    "Plans embed their own validation (Validation Commands + tests + steps-to-reproduce); agents can and do check their own work — but you still manually verify.",
    "THINK HARD–style reasoning activation is a leverage point: deliberately buy more compute for planning-grade work.",
    "The same slash-command template runs interactively AND headlessly (claude -p + stream-json → JSONL). That symmetry is the bridge from this lesson to AI developer workflows.",
    "Start now, small: run /chore on something real today; 'my codebase is too big' is a named limiting belief, and specialization of templates is the answer to scale."

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "What was once a complete joke is now the most valuable skill any engineer can have. The prompt is everything.", "approx_timestamp": "0:18" },
    { "text": "It's a plan. It's a specification. It's a PRD. Plans are prompts scaled up for high impact.", "approx_timestamp": "1:46" },
    { "text": "The plan is the prompt. And that means great planning is great prompting.", "approx_timestamp": "1:52" },
    { "text": "Those who plan the future tend to create it. Success is planned.", "approx_timestamp": "2:46" },
    { "text": "With just three tactics, you'll learn the Pareto 80/20 of agentic engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "2:59" },
    { "text": "When you template your engineering, you encode your problem solving into reusable units that you, your team, and your agents can see, use, and importantly, improve.", "approx_timestamp": "3:40" },
    { "text": "What is a meta prompt? It's a prompt that builds a prompt.", "approx_timestamp": "8:04" },
    { "text": "Not only should we stop coding, we should also lean into and leverage our agent to write plans with us and for us.", "approx_timestamp": "11:40" },
    { "text": "It doesn't take a lot to do a lot, but you need the right information.", "approx_timestamp": "12:40" },
    { "text": "This is a higher order prompt, AKA a hop.", "approx_timestamp": "13:34" },
    { "text": "Don't limit yourself. Don't make the mistake in thinking that Gen AI can't solve your problem in a major way.", "approx_timestamp": "18:19" },
    { "text": "Why do I keep opening up new Claude Code instances?... I keep opening new terminals and starting fresh agent instances that have no memory of what just happened.", "approx_timestamp": "23:03" },
    { "text": "We force our prompts, plans and templates to be isolated, reusable, and improvable assets with zero dependencies.", "approx_timestamp": "25:34" },
    { "text": "Remember, we're not here to babysit a single agent.", "approx_timestamp": "25:55" },
    { "text": "We need to decouple our performance from the conversational context window.", "approx_timestamp": "26:26" },
    { "text": "We want one shot successes.", "approx_timestamp": "26:32" },
    { "text": "This is the power of templating your engineering. I still haven't lifted a finger.", "approx_timestamp": "30:24" },

  "what_student_must_internalize": [
    "The plan IS the prompt. A plan/spec/PRD is a prompt scaled up for high impact — so great planning is literally great prompting, not a separate discipline.",
    "Templates encode problem-solving for CLASSES of work, not instances. /chore, /bug, /feature each encode a different process; the output of a template is always a plan in specs/, never code.",
    "A meta prompt is a prompt that builds a prompt; a higher order prompt (HOP) is a prompt that takes prompts as input. Template → plan → /implement(plan) is meta-prompting composed with a HOP.",
    "Two prompts, two phases, two agents: planning and building are separate SDLC nodes run by separate fresh instances. The chore was completed 'agentically with two prompts, one for the planning phase and one for the coding building phase.'",
    "The three reasons for fresh agents: context focus; isolated/reusable/improvable zero-dependency assets; preparation for off-device runs. Decouple performance from the conversational context window; aim for one-shot successes.",
    "At boot you should know 100% of your agent's context (the HOP file + the plan file). That certainty is what makes failures diagnosable and templates improvable.",
    "Plans embed their own validation (Validation Commands + tests + steps-to-reproduce); agents can and do check their own work — but you still manually verify.",
    "THINK HARD–style reasoning activation is a leverage point: deliberately buy more compute for planning-grade work.",
    "The same slash-command template runs interactively AND headlessly (claude -p + stream-json → JSONL). That symmetry is the bridge from this lesson to AI developer workflows.",
    "Start now, small: run /chore on something real today; 'my codebase is too big' is a named limiting belief, and specialization of templates is the answer to scale."
  ],

1	# TAC-1 · Hello Agentic Coding — Master Teaching Notes
2	
3	> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 21:51 · Beginner · Tactic #1: **Stop Coding**
4	> Lesson artifact: a 35-line README, one settings file, and three ~20-line launcher scripts. That's the whole codebase, on purpose.
5	
6	**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** AI coding (generating code from prompts) was phase one; agentic coding — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tools inside a programmable agent — is phase two, and the engineer who commands it becomes irreplaceable by replacing themselves.
7	
8	**The chapter must land eight ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## Idea 1 — A new role exists: the Agentic Engineer
13	
14	**Hook.** In 2023, before it was obvious, Dan bought a domain name as a bet: agenticengineer.com. The bet was that a new software role would emerge, defined not by writing code but by *building systems that can take actions as we can*. > Lesson artifact: a 35-line README, one settings file, and three ~20-line launcher scripts. That's the whole codebase, on purpose.

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** AI coding (generating code from prompts) was phase one; agentic coding — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tools inside a programmable agent — is phase two, and the engineer who commands it becomes irreplaceable by replacing themselves.

**The chapter must land eight ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.

---

## Idea 1 — A new role exists: the Agentic Engineer

**Hook.** In 2023, before it was obvious, Dan bought a domain name as a bet: agenticengineer.com. The bet was that a new software role would emerge, defined not by writing code but by *building systems that can take actions as we can*. Lesson 1 opens by declaring the bet settled: the role now exists, and this course exists to move you into it.

**Picture.** Frame t0078 (1:18): the agenticengineer.com page on screen while Dan narrates the 2023 prediction. Frame t0115 (1:55): the two-phase timeline — Phase 1 "AI CODING" (vibe coders born, code commoditized) flowing into Phase 2 "AGENTIC CODING" (real engineers strike back).

**Failure mode.** Hearing "new role" as a title change rather than a job change. The weak student keeps doing phase-1 work (prompt → code → paste) with a new label. # TAC-3 · Success is Planned — Master Teaching Notes

> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 46:32 · Intermediate · Tactic #3: **Template Your Engineering**
> Lesson artifact: eight slash-command files in `.claude/commands/` — four of them (chore/bug/feature/implement) are the entire tactic. The app underneath (the lesson-2 NL→SQL client/server) is deliberately just a workbench.

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** A plan is a prompt scaled up — so encode HOW you plan each class of work (chores, bugs, features) into reusable templates that agents fill out, execute the resulting plans with fresh memory-less agents via a higher-order `/implement`, and you've templated your engineering into a system that can eventually run without you.

**The chapter must land ten ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.

---

## Idea 1 — The prompt is everything, and a plan is a prompt scaled up

**Hook.** "What was once a complete joke is now the most valuable skill any engineer can have." Prompting got laughed at; then it became the medium through which all work flows to agents. So ask the question the lesson opens with: *what does a scaled prompt look like?* It's a plan. It's a specification. It's a PRD.

**Picture.** Frame t0116 (1:56): the on-screen equation **Great Planning === Great Prompting** overlaid on the keyboard shot — the thesis as one image.

**Worked example.** `specs/init_nlq_to_sql_to_table.md` ships in the repo: the 749-line plan that *built the entire application* in lesson 2. The proof that plans are executable prompts is sitting on disk before you type anything.

**Dan's term.** *Plans are prompts scaled up for high impact. The plan is the prompt.* Corollary later in the lesson: plans are *"staging environments for code"* — engineering work compressed into natural language that the agent expands.

**Failure mode.** Treating plans as documentation (write-once, goes stale in a wiki) instead of as the actual instruction fired into an agent. The tell: a student who "writes a plan" and then re-explains everything to the agent in chat has not connected plan=prompt.

**Retrieval Q.** Complete the ladder: prompt → ? → ? — and state the two Dan equalities. *(Prompt → plan/spec/PRD → template; the plan is the prompt; great planning is great prompting.)*

---

## Idea 2 — Tactic #3: Template Your Engineering

**Hook.** Planning alone is expensive: it's time-consuming, there's always something to miss, and the cost scales with problem difficulty and codebase size. You could write every plan by hand forever — or you could encode *how you plan* once, and let agents write the plans.

**Picture.** Frame t0200 (3:20): the full Tactic 03 slide — definition, the 01–08 tactic dot grid (this is tactic three of eight), and the **Daily Actions** sidebar (use meta-prompts for problem classes; create specialized templates; build HOPs that pass plans into plans; review and refine templates from outcomes; document domain-specific patterns; convert successful prompts into meta-prompts).

**Worked example.** The whole of `.claude/commands/`: chore.md (53 lines), bug.md (69), feature.md (91), implement.md (12). Zero application code — pure encoded process. Also the sleeper example: `/install` runs `scripts/copy_dot_env.sh` agentically ("we're having an agent with a reusable prompt do this work for us") — reuse all the way down.

**Dan's term.** *Template your engineering* — "you encode your problem solving into reusable units that you, your team, and your agents can see, use, and importantly, improve." Solves problem **classes**, not problems; explicitly "one of many solutions to the my-codebase-is-too-big problem" and one of the 12 leverage points.

**Failure mode.** Hearing "template" as code boilerplate/snippets. These templates contain no code — the output of a template is a *plan*. Second failure: copying the templates into your repo without rewriting `Relevant Files`, so the agent researches files that don't exist and produces mush.

**Retrieval Q.** What does a template output, and for whom (three audiences)? *(A plan in specs/; for you, your team, and your agents — to see, use, and improve.)*

---

## Idea 3 — The meta prompt: one sentence in, a 64-line plan out

**Hook.** Dan types one sentence — *"Replace all server print statements with proper python logging. Use proper log levels. Preserve the exact same log output. Make sure all output is written standard out"* (as typed on screen) — and walks away. The agent reads the README, researches the codebase with its reasoning model, and writes a complete plan.

**Picture.** Frame t0470 (7:50): the `/chore` prompt being typed (with install.md's 11 lines above it). Frame t0585 (9:45): the payoff — `Write(specs/replace-print-with-logging.md)`, "Wrote 64 lines", the plan excerpt inventorying prints by line number, and the one-sentence prompt circled underneath.

**Worked example.** The generated plan (not committed; regenerate it in the lab) inventories the codebase's actual print statements — 18 lines in `app/server/server.py` plus 1 in `app/server/main.py` = 19, each with its line number and message type. (Accuracy note for the chapter: the on-camera agent's *prose summary* says "19 in server.py / 20 across 2 files" while its own line inventory totals 18+1 — quote the inventory, not the prose.)

**Dan's term.** *Meta prompt* — "a prompt that builds a prompt. More specifically, this agentic prompt builds a plan based on a template that our agent fills out." Your input is a *high-level prompt* — "a prompt that's void of detail."

**Failure mode.** Expecting `/chore` to fix the code. It plans only; nothing in the app changes until `/implement` runs. Students who "finish" after the plan generated have done half the workflow; students who tell the same session "now do it" have skipped the fresh-agent discipline (Idea 7).

**Retrieval Q.** Define meta prompt, and name the demo's input and output artifacts. *(A prompt that builds a prompt; input: one-sentence chore string into $ARGUMENTS; output: specs/replace-print-with-logging.md, a 64-line plan.)*

---

## Idea 4 — Template anatomy: five parts, three specializations, one home

**Hook.** Open `chore.md` expecting something exotic; find "a reusable prompt that looks ordinary" — yet "the instructions in this prompt completely change your engineering impact."

**Picture.** Frame t0660 (11:00): chore.md lines 1–34 fully legible — purpose sentence, Instructions (with `THINK HARD`), Relevant Files, and the opening of Plan Format.

**Worked example.** The shared skeleton across chore/bug/feature: (1) **purpose line** at top ("Create a new plan in specs/*.md to resolve the `Chore` using the exact specified markdown `Plan Format`..."); (2) **## Instructions** — thorough-but-precise, name the file appropriately, "IMPORTANT: Replace every <placeholder>", "Use your reasoning model: THINK HARD", "Start your research by reading the `README.md` file"; (3) **## Relevant Files** — README.md, app/**, scripts/** and "Ignore all other files in the codebase."; (4) **## Plan Format** — the exact markdown skeleton in a ```md fence; (5) the final H2 (## Chore / ## Bug / ## Feature) holding **$ARGUMENTS**. The specializations encode different engineering: bug.md adds Problem/Solution Statements, Steps to Reproduce, Root Cause Analysis and demands a surgical minimal fix ("Don't use decorators. Keep it simple."); feature.md adds a User Story, a 3-phase Implementation Plan, Testing Strategy, and Acceptance Criteria. All plans land in `specs/`.

**Dan's term.** *Plan format* / *giving our agent a template*; the `$ARGUMENTS` slot is "the Claude Code argument parameter that just takes whatever we passed in."

**Failure mode.** One-format-fits-all thinking — flattening bug and feature planning into the chore shape and losing exactly the sections (repro, root cause, acceptance criteria) that make those work classes safe. Also: deleting the seeded validation line (`cd app/server && uv run pytest`) when porting, which silently removes the plan's self-check floor.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the five structural parts every template shares, and two sections bug.md adds that chore.md lacks. *(Purpose, Instructions, Relevant Files, Plan Format, $ARGUMENTS slot; Steps to Reproduce + Root Cause Analysis — also Problem/Solution Statements.)*

---

## Idea 5 — The Higher Order Prompt: /implement runs any plan

**Hook.** The build phase needs a prompt too — and it's 12 lines. "It doesn't take a lot to do a lot, but you need the right information."

**Picture.** Frame t0815 (13:35): the HOP definition slide — verbatim: *"A prompt that accepts other prompts as input parameters, enabling composable agentic workflows. Higher order prompts (HOPs) allow you to pass plans, templates, or other prompts into reusable execution frameworks - like passing functions into functions in programming languages, but for agentic systems."* — with implement.md's `## Plan` / `$ARGUMENTS` visible behind it and the logging diff already flowing.

**Worked example.** `.claude/commands/implement.md` in full: purpose ("Follow the `Instructions` to implement the `Plan` then `Report` the completed work."), one instruction ("Read the plan, think hard about the plan and implement the plan."), `## Plan` → `$ARGUMENTS`, `## Report` → bullet summary + "Report the files and total lines changed with `git diff --stat`". Invocation: `/implement specs/replace-print-with-logging.md`. The same 12 lines later run the bug plan unchanged — and Dan sketches HOP variants: "read your plan, implemented it... after you implement, review the work completed against the plan."

**Dan's term.** *Higher order prompt, AKA a hop* — "plans getting passed into plans"; like higher-order functions. The chore completes "agentically with two prompts, one for the planning phase and one for the coding building phase."

**Failure mode.** Bloating the executor. Students stuff plan-specific detail into implement.md, coupling it to one plan and killing its universality — detail belongs in the plan (or template), the HOP stays generic. Also: forgetting the Report block exists, then complaining the run "ended silently."

**Retrieval Q.** What are implement.md's four sections, and why does its smallness matter? *(Purpose/Instructions/Plan($ARGUMENTS)/Report; because it's a universal executor — the power flows through it from the plan, so it must stay generic.)*

---

## Idea 6 — THINK HARD: buying reasoning compute on purpose

**Hook.** Both the templates and the executor contain a strange all-caps phrase: THINK HARD. It's not motivation — it's a switch.

**Picture.** Frame t0660 shows it in chore.md's instructions ("Use your reasoning model: THINK HARD about the plan..."); the implement run banner shows thinking-mode workings ("Schlepping… / Philosophising…" with token counts).

**Worked example.** implement.md line 5: "Read the plan, think hard about the plan and implement the plan." Dan: "We're activating Claude Code's information dense keyword to activate the reasoning model... If you just search for think, you'll be able to find this. This is an information dense keyword that Anthropic has encoded into this word here. Think."

**Dan's term.** *Information dense keyword*; framed as one of the *12 leverage points* — "We always wanna throw more compute at the problem, right? Especially as we start to scale this up."

**Failure mode.** Cargo-culting the words without the principle (sprinkling "think hard" on trivial work), or the reverse — running planning-grade work with reasoning off to save tokens and getting shallow plans. The durable principle: match reasoning budget to problem difficulty; planning is where it pays.

**Retrieval Q.** What does "think hard" do in course-era Claude Code, and what's the transferable principle? *(Activates the reasoning model via an information-dense keyword; deliberately allocate more reasoning compute to planning-grade work.)*

---

## Idea 7 — Fresh agents every time: three reasons, four KPIs, one certainty

**Hook.** "Why do I keep opening up new Claude Code instances? Look at all these terminals... fresh agent instances that have no memory of what just happened. Why am I doing that? Don't we want to keep rolling the important context...? **No.**"

**Picture.** Frame t1390 (23:10): implement.md on screen, the agent's todo checklist mirroring the bug plan's steps 1:1, and a right rail stacked with eight terminal sessions.

**Worked example.** Six separate agent boots in one lesson: /install; /chore; /implement (chore); /bug; /implement (bug); the headless /feature run. Between phases Dan commits specs + code ("you want each one of these steps to commit their changes" — full Git discipline promised for later lessons).

**Dan's term.** The three reasons, verbatim targets: (1) *"we free up our context — focus every available token on the task at hand"* (agents have context windows; so do overloaded humans); (2) *"we force our prompts, plans, and templates to be isolated, reusable, and improvable assets with zero dependencies"* — creating "a trail of success or a trail of things we can improve"; (3) *"we prepare for true off-device agentic coding."* KPI linkage (from lesson 2): size ↑, attempts ↓, streak ↑, presence → 0 — *"we need to decouple our performance from the conversational context window"*; *"we want one shot successes"*; *"we're not here to babysit a single agent."* And the certainty: booting from implement.md + a plan file means "I know 100%... what the agent's perspective is."

**Failure mode.** The comfort of the rolling conversation. It feels safer ("the agent remembers!") but it builds assets that secretly depend on chat history — irreproducible by teammates, unimprovable, and impossible off-device. The tell: "it worked yesterday in my session" with no way to say what the agent knew.

**Retrieval Q.** Recite the three reasons and the KPI the pattern ultimately drives to zero. *(Context focus; isolated/reusable/improvable zero-dependency assets; preparing for off-device — presence → 0.)*

---

## Idea 8 — Plans that check themselves (and the human who still checks)

**Hook.** Near the end of the bug implement, the agent runs a diff over its own work, announces two issues, and fixes them — unprompted. "This is the power of templating your engineering. I still haven't lifted a finger."

**Picture.** Frame t0945 (15:45): the logging diff — red `print(f"[SUCCESS]...")` → green `logger.info(...)` under the plan's step list with exact line numbers. Frame t1285 (21:25): the bug plan's Root Cause Analysis (keyword blocklist insufficient; identifiers trusted from uploads; SQLite params don't cover identifiers; no centralized SQL layer), Relevant Files, and `### New Files` → `app/server/core/sql_security.py`.

**Worked example.** Every Plan Format ends with **## Validation Commands** ("Execute every command to validate... with zero regressions", seeded with `cd app/server && uv run pytest`; chore.md adds "Don't validate with curl commands."), and the last step of every Step-by-Step Tasks list is running them. The bug plan adds Steps to Reproduce so a human can verify independently — which Dan does: restarts the app, tries an injection-shaped concat query, re-runs pytest by hand. All four Relevant-Files claims in the generated bug plan are literally true of the shipped code (raw `cursor.execute(sql_query)` behind a substring blocklist in sql_processor.py; f-string identifiers in file_processor.py and insights.py; `cursor.execute(f"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS {table_name}")` at server.py:243).

**Dan's term.** *Self-validating loops with tests*; "it's checking its own work — self validation." Flagged as "a huge, huge leverage point... it has its own dedicated lesson."

**Failure mode.** Both extremes: trusting self-validation totally (skipping the manual repro, letting a subtly wrong fix land), or ignoring it (deleting Validation Commands when porting templates, so plans stop being closed-loop). The video's own numbers teach calibration: Dan's run reports 52 tests / 18 new — your regenerated run will differ; the invariant is zero regressions + new coverage, not magic numbers.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the two self-validation mechanisms in the demo and the one human step Dan still performs. *(Embedded Validation Commands (pytest + running the apps) and the agent's own git-diff review-and-fix; Dan still manually reproduces — browser query + pytest.)*

---

## Idea 9 — The off-device preview: claude -p, stream-json, and an invisible agent

**Hook.** "We won't be able to open up the terminal" — if features are to ship end-to-end without us, the agent must run where we aren't. So Dan fires the /feature template with no visible agent at all, and watches a file grow.

**Picture.** Frame t2205 (36:45): the complete command — `claude -p "/feature \"Create a new query history side panel...\"" --output-format stream-json --dangerously-skip-permissions --model opus --verbose > feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl`. Frame t2270 (37:50): the JSONL appending live — system init, assistant events with `claude-opus-4-20250514`, tool results. Frame t2575 (42:55): the deliverable — `specs/query-history-panel.md` rendered (Feature Description, User Story, Problem Statement...), written by an agent nobody watched.

**Worked example.** The exact same `.claude/commands/feature.md` template runs interactively and headlessly — that symmetry is the entire bridge to lesson 4. Dan's scoping on the scary flag: "running in dangerously skip permissions. This is going to work just fine for now. It's very low risk" — a planning-only run in a demo repo. The output redirect is the composition hook: "we can chain these agents together. We can check their output."

**Dan's term.** *Claude Code in its programmatic form*; "this prompt here represents the planning phase" of the SDLC → *agentic software development lifecycle*; destination named: *AI developer workflows* — "the highest composition level and the greatest leverage point of agentic coding" (lesson 4: "let your product ship itself").

**Failure mode.** Two: treating `--dangerously-skip-permissions` as the default posture everywhere (it was scoped risk, not habit — modern practice uses allowlists/sandboxes/hooks); and dismissing the JSONL as "just logs" when it's the machine-readable interface another program or agent consumes.

**Retrieval Q.** Which template ran headlessly, with which four flags, into which file — and what appeared in specs/? *(/feature; --output-format stream-json, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --model opus, --verbose; > feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl; specs/query-history-panel.md.)*

---

## Idea 10 — Specialize, share, start now: templates as differentiation

**Hook.** Codex, Copilot, Devin, Jules, Gemini CLI "and whatever comes next" — great tools, but "no matter how great AI gets, they don't understand your codebase like you do." The granularity you need lives in templates you write.

**Picture.** Frame t2575 doubles here: a comprehensive feature plan produced by *your* encoded process is the differentiation argument made visible.

**Worked example.** The specialization ladder Dan sketches over the generic trio: a front-end feature template for specific page sets; a chore template for your database migration system; a bug resolver for your research-notebook system. Team leverage: templates are time savers "not just for you, but for your entire team" — see/use/improve. And the improvement loop: as your size-KPI grows, templates get bigger or more precise — "we get this self-improving loop inside of your codebase."

**Dan's term.** *"The more custom your templates are, the more unique your engineering gets"* — and the standing order: *"You want to be building the system that builds the system."* Anti-pattern named: *"Having agents run loose on your codebase without structure, without knowing how you do things is a plan for failure."* Objection pre-handled: "my codebase is too big" is *a limiting belief*.

**Failure mode.** Waiting. The lesson's explicit CTA is to run one small `/chore` today ("Do not wait... Don't wait to complete this course. You'll miss out on getting ahead now") — the aha moment is engineered to be cheap. The meta-failure is perfectionism: polishing a mega-template before ever firing one.

**Retrieval Q.** Why do custom templates beat out-of-the-box agent tools, per Dan — and what is the lesson's call to action? *(Tools don't know your codebase or give SDLC-granular control; encode YOUR practice. CTA: run one small /chore now.)*

---

## Timeline map (VTT-verified)

| t | beat |
